FEDERATED SWARM LEARNING FOR PERSONALIZED BCI AT THE LIMIT STARLI RESEARCH WORKS | INSTITUTE XXIV | FLAGSHIP 23 Feng Cheng-en 33 × Starli PUBLICATION DESCRIPTION (COPY-READY) Can brain–computer interface systems learn from multiple laboratories and microrobotic sensing platforms without transferring raw neural recordings, reproducing device-specific shortcuts, or sacrificing the least-represented participants? This research monograph explores that question through the coupling of local swarm learning, privacy-preserving collaboration, and out-of-site generalization. The volume treats federation as a testable scientific and governance architecture—not an automatic privacy guarantee. It distinguishes confidential transport, secure aggregation, formal differential privacy, machine-unlearning claims, and genuine downstream withdrawal of model influence. It examines non-identically distributed neural data, sensor drift, personalized calibration, negative transfer, client-level poisoning, subgroup equity, and the difficult question of who may authorize a model update or a subsequent BCI-mediated action. Its research structure includes 30 linked mathematical derivation and definition plates; 82 chapters, each with five separately paginated research sections; 200 detailed Research Gates that offer future investigators falsifiable experimental entry points; and 33 Phoenix Answer Embryos designed for revision, disconfirmation, and scientific handoff. A 20-record DOI evidence ledger anchors established methods while keeping proposed neurovascular microrobot integrations clearly distinct from demonstrated evidence. The central research challenge is not simply to improve average federated accuracy. It is to determine when shared structure remains predictive at previously unseen sites, when local autonomy is the scientifically stronger answer, and when the responsible choice is to abstain, revert, or retire a model. This is a non-clinical, hypothesis-generating research atlas, not evidence of validated human neurovascular microrobots, a clinically proven BCI, or guaranteed data privacy
